\begin{abstract}
Oxford Nanopore adaptive sampling (``Read Until'') requires a client to decide, within a
physical deadline, whether to eject a molecule still transiting the pore. We make two
contributions. First, the decision budget is not the obstacle: a single-process C++20
data plane with single-copy ingestion, zero-copy propagation, lock-free single-producer
single-consumer rings and a reference-counting arena protocol reaches a median per-chunk
decision latency of 124.8 µs [115.6--132.3] against a derived service bound of 1.56 ms, at
3.70 GiB peak resident set over a 64 Mb reference index of 63.9 M minimizers, sustaining
604--645 chunk/s with zero drops across nine 40 s runs. For calibration, the bare orchestration
layer of a basecalling client (readfish with a no-operation caller) costs 124.3 µs per
read-chunk on the same rig---indistinguishable from our \emph{complete} signal-space decision.
Second, we locate the real limit. We frame Read Until as a soft-real-time
\emph{loss system}, in which a mean comfortably inside budget is consistent with an arbitrary
deadline-miss rate, and we report a distribution against a derived budget rather than a mean.
Our pipeline resolves 17.6\% [16.6--18.8] of reads at a zero-false-positive threshold where
RawHash2 resolves 91.8\% [91.2--92.4] on identical input. We account for this gap without
appeal to the decision rule. We proposed a seed-survival law $P(\mathrm{key}) = a^{E}$ in the
per-event bucket agreement $a$ and key length $E$, argued it was a lower bound, and then
\emph{refuted our own bound}: once event retention is data-dependent the governing form is
$P(\mathrm{key}) \approx (1-g)^{E} a^{E}$, where $g$ is the rate at which the two event
sequences fail to correspond at all. Under one estimator on identical input at
realistic motor-dwell dispersion, RawHash2 achieves $a = 0.911$, $g = 0.092$ at $E = 8$,
giving $P(\mathrm{key}) = 0.254$ and 467 anchors per read, against our $a = 0.783$,
$g = 0.196$ at $E = 12$, giving 0.0055 and 14.9 anchors. The 46-fold key-match difference
decomposes into $9.3\times$ from encoding and segmentation and $4.9\times$ from key length; anchor supply
differs 31-fold. Three measured root causes follow: asymmetric event retention between
reference and query encoders, a quantiser that spends too little alphabet on agreement, and
recoverable loss inside the chainer.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
nanopore sequencing, adaptive sampling, soft real-time systems, lock-free data structures,
raw signal mapping, quantisation
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

Nanopore sequencing reads a molecule as it translocates a pore, emitting an ionic current trace
in real time. Because the molecule is still in the pore while data arrives, the instrument
exposes an interface---Read Until---that lets a client request ejection of a molecule it does
not want, freeing the channel for another. The economic case is direct: on-target yield rises
without changing library preparation.

The interface imposes a deadline that is physical rather than conventional. Signal arrives in
chunks at a fixed cadence, and a chunk describes bases that have \emph{already} passed through
the pore. A decision delivered after the molecule has finished translocating has no value at
all; it does not merely arrive late. With $C$ active channels delivering a chunk every $T_c$
seconds, and a tolerance of $W$ chunks before the decision is worthless, the admissible mean
service time per decision is
\[ S < \frac{W \cdot T_c}{C} \]
which at $W = 2$, $C = 512$ and $T_c = 0.4$ s gives 1.5625 ms, hereafter 1.56 ms.

Two framings follow, and the paper is organised around them.

\textbf{Soft real time.} Utility falls to zero at the deadline rather than degrading smoothly.
This makes the \emph{distribution} of decision latency, not its mean, the quantity of interest.

\textbf{A loss system, not a delay system.} Under saturation a client must choose between
queueing work and discarding it. Queueing converts decisions that would have been useful into
decisions that arrive too late, so dropping is correct rather than merely pragmatic. The
consequence for evaluation is sharp and, we argue, under-appreciated: \textbf{a mean
comfortably inside the budget is consistent with an arbitrary deadline-miss rate.} A system
reporting ``mean 124 µs against a 1.56 ms budget'' has said nothing about whether it meets its
deadline.

Existing Read Until work does report latency, in two forms: signal consumed before a decision
(mean bases or chunks per read), and mean processing time per read. What we did not find in the
systems we surveyed is a deadline-miss rate against a stated service bound, a latency
distribution with tail percentiles, or the fraction of decisions arriving too late to act on.
That gap---reporting a distribution against a derived budget, with the instrument and
environment characterised well enough for the tail to carry meaning---motivates the first half
of this paper.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item A lock-free soft-real-time data plane for signal-space adaptive sampling, with a
reference-counting arena protocol that makes reset-under-dispatch unrepresentable by
construction rather than by a timing assumption (Section~\ref{sec:plane}), evaluated as a
distribution against a derived budget over nine runs (Section~\ref{sec:eval}).
\item A negative result, explained rather than excused: our pipeline is $5.2\times$ less accurate
than a published signal-space mapper on identical input, and we locate the cause before
seeding (Section~\ref{sec:gap}).
\item A seed-survival law, including the refutation of our own earlier formulation of it, and
an estimator-symmetric measurement of its two parameters for both systems
(Section~\ref{sec:law}).
\item Three measured root causes and the design prescriptions that follow
(Section~\ref{sec:causes}).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{What this paper does not claim.} We do not claim competitive mapping accuracy; we
report 17.6\% against 91.8\% and explain it. We do not claim a novel matching method;
quantised-event hashing is established~\cite{rawhash,rawhash2}. We do not claim trustworthy
tail latency: every measurement here was taken under a hypervisor, and Section~\ref{sec:limits}
scopes what that permits. All signal is simulated.

\section{Background and related work}

\textbf{The interface.} MinKNOW~\cite{minknow} exposes a bidirectional streaming RPC delivering
raw signal chunks per channel and accepting actions. Read identity is carried by a string; a
numeric read index was removed from the API in version 6.0, which constrains client-side data
structures.

\textbf{Basecalling clients.} readfish~\cite{readfish} and similar clients basecall each chunk
and map the resulting sequence. This is accurate and reuses mature tooling, but places a neural
network and a sequence aligner~\cite{minimap2} inside the decision loop.

\textbf{Signal-space mappers} avoid basecalling by encoding the reference into expected signal
under a pore model and matching quantised query events directly. UNCALLED~\cite{uncalled} uses
an FM-index over events; Sigmap~\cite{sigmap} and RawHash~\cite{rawhash} use seed-and-chain
over quantised event $k$-mers; RawHash2~\cite{rawhash2} adds an adaptive quantiser;
RawAlign~\cite{rawalign} adds alignment to seeding; Sigmoni~\cite{sigmoni} classifies with an
$r$-index over a small picoamp alphabet. A recent benchmarking framework,
RawBench~\cite{rawbench}, decomposes raw signal analysis into reference encoding, segmentation,
and matching, and evaluates three segmentation methods---t-test changepoint detection,
basecaller move tables, and a learned segmenter. We adopt that decomposition, splitting
matching into quantisation, seeding and chaining, because our argument needs that granularity.

\textbf{The pipeline is ordered, and earlier stages bound later ones.} Reference encoding
$\rightarrow$ segmentation $\rightarrow$ quantisation $\rightarrow$ seeding $\rightarrow$
chaining. No chaining strategy can recover evidence that quantisation destroyed. This
observation is the spine of Sections~\ref{sec:gap}--\ref{sec:causes}.

\textbf{Streaming decision structures.} Misra--Gries~\cite{misragries} and
Space-Saving~\cite{spacesaving} maintain approximate frequent items in bounded space. We use a
set-associative variant whose update cost is $O(\text{ways})$ rather than
$O(\text{counters})$, which matters on a decision path.

\textbf{Simulation.} Squigulator~\cite{squigulator} generates signal with configurable
dwell-time dispersion; its default is a coefficient of variation of approximately 0.44.
Icarust~\cite{icarust} serves a live Read Until API but emits a fixed sample count per
$k$-mer, so it produces the CV $= 0$ case exactly; we patched it to draw lognormal dwell.

\section{The data plane}
\label{sec:plane}

\subsection{Design constraints}

Four constraints shape the design. The decision path must not allocate, because an allocator
excursion is unbounded. It must not take a lock, because a blocked worker holds a deadline it
cannot meet. State must be $O(\text{channels})$ with compile-time per-channel constants,
because read length is set by library preparation and is not observable in advance. And
backpressure must discard rather than queue, for the loss-system reason of Section~I.

\subsection{Single-copy ingestion, zero-copy propagation}

Signal is copied exactly once, by the protobuf runtime, into arena-backed storage at the
transport boundary. Nothing downstream copies signal again. Workers receive a 56-byte borrowed
descriptor holding an absolute sample index, borrowed pointers into arena-owned
read-identifier and payload storage, the owning arena slot, a receive timestamp, and a narrow
tail of lengths and type codes. Declared in natural reading order the structure is 72 bytes;
field-ordered for size it is 56, and a compile-time assertion that it does not straddle a
cacheline is what caught the difference.

Two narrowings are guarded at ingest. Chunk length drops from 64 to 32 bits because a chunk is
sub-second and $2^{32}$ samples is about twelve days at 4 kHz. The read-identifier length drops
to 16 bits because identifiers are 36-character UUIDs. The absolute sample index is
deliberately \emph{not} narrowed: a 72-hour run at 4 kHz already reaches ${\approx}10^9$,
uncomfortably close to $2^{32}$.

\subsection{The arena reference-counting protocol}

The hazard is reset-under-dispatch: an arena slot recycled while a descriptor referring to it
is still in a ring. Because the memory remains mapped and arena-owned, the failure is silent
payload corruption rather than a crash.

The protocol removes it structurally (Figure~\ref{fig:arena}). \texttt{acquire()} returns a
slot at refcount 1, and that initial reference is held by the \textbf{reader}, not by a
consumer. The reader pushes descriptors to $n$ shard rings, raising the count to $1 + n$, and
only then releases its own. The count can therefore reach zero only after every worker
reference has been taken and dropped, and the slot cannot be reset while any dispatch is
outstanding. No bound on how long a worker takes is required.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[

  state/.style={draw, rounded corners=3pt, align=center, font=\small,
                minimum height=8mm, inner sep=2pt, fill=blue!4},
  free/.style={state, fill=black!4},
  lbl/.style={font=\scriptsize, align=center}]
\node[free] (f) {FREE\\[-1pt]\scriptsize count 0};
\node[state, right=12mm of f] (a) {ACQUIRED\\[-1pt]\scriptsize count 1, reader};
\node[state, right=12mm of a] (d) {DISPATCHED\\[-1pt]\scriptsize count $1{+}n$};
\node[state, below=9mm of d] (r) {DRAINING\\[-1pt]\scriptsize count $n$};
\draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (f) -- node[lbl, above]{acquire()} node[lbl,below]{$+1$} (a);
\draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (a) -- node[lbl, above]{push to rings} node[lbl,below]{$+n$} (d);
\draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (d) -- node[lbl, right, xshift=1mm]{\parbox{20mm}{reader
  release(), \emph{after} all $n$ exist}} (r);
\draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (r.west) -- ++(-28mm,0) node[lbl, above, midway]
  {last worker release() $\rightarrow$ 0} |- (f.south);
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Arena slot lifetime. The reader holding the initial reference is what makes
reset-under-dispatch unrepresentable: the count cannot reach zero while a descriptor is still

\label{fig:arena}

\subsection{Lock-free handoff and sharding}

Handoff uses single-producer single-consumer rings with free-running 64-bit counters and
power-of-two capacity, so the index is a mask rather than a modulus and the full capacity is
usable rather than capacity $-\,1$. Producer and consumer each cache the other's index,
removing cross-core loads from the unsaturated steady state; head, tail and both cached copies
are separately cacheline-aligned. Shard rings hold 2048 descriptors; action rings hold 1024. At
four shards the rings total under 0.75 MB, negligible beside the index.

Chunks are sharded by \texttt{channel \& mask}, so all per-channel state is reached by exactly
one thread \textbf{by construction}. This is what makes the lock-free claim cheap: there is no
shared mutable per-channel state to protect. Backpressure is drop-never-block, with the
invariant $\textit{offered} = \textit{pushed} + \textit{dropped}$ maintained by counters.

\subsection{Bounded per-channel state}

The decision structure dominates per-channel state. The set-associative vote table is
$64 \times 4 \times 12$ B $=$ 3,072 B per channel (1.57 MB at 512 channels, 8.22 MB at 2675);
its update cost is $O(4)$ rather than the $O(256)$ a classical Misra--Gries table of the same
counter count would pay on the decision path, and its expected retention threshold is $m/320$
against $m/257$. The anchor-history chainer is $1024 \times 14$ B $=$ 14,336 B per channel.
Every figure is a compile-time constant times the channel count; nothing depends on read length
or elapsed run time.

\subsection{Thread topology}

Threads are placed from the kernel's SMT sibling sets rather than from processor-index
arithmetic. This is not fussiness: our measurement host enumerates siblings adjacently
(\texttt{0-1 2-3 4-5 6-7}), so an earlier rule that gave each role ``the next logical
processor'' placed the reader and writer on \emph{the same physical core} while two whole cores
sat idle. The relationship is not portable. At two shards the data plane is four threads
(reader, writer, two workers), which fits four physical cores; at four shards it is six, which
does not.

\section{Evaluation of the data plane}
\label{sec:eval}

\subsection{Method and instrumentation}

Latency is the interval from the transport read returning to the decision being reached,
recorded with HdrHistogram~\cite{hdrhistogram} at three significant figures, bounding relative
error at 0.1\%. The recorder reports its own backend on every line, so a degraded estimate
cannot be mistaken for a measurement.

This instrumentation is a correction. An earlier power-of-two histogram reported four 99th
percentiles of 111.93, 112.12, 223.66 and 447.59 µs across four runs. At the host's calibrated
invariant TSC frequency of 2418.7 MHz the only values representable in that range are 54.19,
108.38, 216.76 and 433.53 µs. Every reported value was a bucket boundary; two runs ``agreeing''
at 112 µs agreed only that the true value lay in [54.19, 108.38]. The general form is worth
stating: \emph{any} instrument whose quantisation is coarse relative to the between-run
variance will report stable values and thereby invite an inference of stability.

The harness records per run the virtualisation status, SMT topology, TSC flags, clocksource,
kernel command line, governor, turbo state, free storage and load average, and refuses to label
a run publishable unless virtualisation is absent, cores are isolated and the governor is set to
performance. Every run reported here carries the development-only label.

\textbf{Host.} Intel Core i5-1135G7, 4 physical cores / 8 logical, under WSL2.
\textbf{Regimes.} R1: a 37 kb reference under constant dwell. R3: a 64 Mb human chr20 reference
under variable dwell at the frozen configuration---4 bits $\times$ 12 events,
minimizer~\cite{minimizers} window
1, detected-event segmentation, two shards, pinned.

processor affinity is about variance, not location.

\subsection{Genome scale: regime R3}

Nine 40 s runs. The daemon's startup line confirms the configuration in every log: 63,981,237
reference bases, geometry $4 \times 12 = 48$-bit keys, window 1, 63,981,218 minimizers,
32,888,127 distinct keys, 512.0 MiB table + 204.3 MiB positions.

Peak resident set is 3.70 GiB in every run---the maximum including the index-build transient;
the steady-state index structures are 716 MiB. Offered chunk arrival is 604--645 per second, set
by the simulator rather than the daemon. \textbf{No chunks were dropped and no deadline misses
were recorded in any of the nine runs.}

At the median this is a utilisation of \textbf{0.080} against the 1.56 ms bound. A 10-chunk read
completes its decisions in \textbf{1.25 ms}---a derivation, ten chunks times the measured median
per-chunk latency, not an independent measurement.

\textbf{The tail is where the loss-system framing earns its place.} Eight of the nine runs sit
strictly inside the budget through the 99.9th percentile, at 1.04--1.40 ms. The ninth does not:
one run reports p99 $=$ 1969.3 µs and p99.9 $=$ 3284.0 µs, and is also the worst of the nine at
p90 and at the mean (Figure~\ref{fig:r3}).

We do not read this as a deadline miss. Across the nine runs the observed \emph{maximum} spans
2.0 ms to 59.4 ms---two orders of magnitude in a quantity the software should not vary in---and,
tellingly, the run with the largest maximum is \textbf{not} the run with the worst p99; its p99
is 630 µs. Maximum and p99 are not correlated here, which is the signature of externally
injected stalls rather than of slow decisions. On a hypervisor without core isolation, this
measurement cannot establish that the system meets its deadline, and cannot establish that it
misses it. Stating that honestly is part of the contribution.

\subsection{Comparison with existing clients}

\textbf{The architectural point.} readfish with a no-operation caller performs no basecalling
and no mapping; 124.3 µs is its orchestration alone, a lower bound on its cost. Our
\emph{complete} signal-space decision over a 64 Mb index costs 124.8 µs. The orchestration layer
of a basecalling client is already as expensive as an entire signal-space decision. This does
not establish superiority---a production readfish does work this configuration omits---but it
does establish that the decision budget is not what stands between signal-space matching and
deployment.

The cost is processor time: 181.5--202.3\% of one core against readfish's 15.6\%, because
workers spin before yielding. We report it alongside.

\textbf{Against a signal-space mapper.} RawHash2, single-threaded on identical reads with the
same pore model, requires 10.64 ms of processor time per read including index load, or 10.18 ms
excluding the load a long-running daemon pays once. Our comparable figure is the derived
1.25 ms. The ratio is $8.2\times$, and must be read with Section~\ref{sec:gap}: a latency ratio between a
system that resolves reads and one that largely does not is a bound on data-plane cost, not a
performance result.

\section{The accuracy gap}
\label{sec:gap}

\subsection{Head-to-head}

Both systems were run on the same 20 Mb chr20 reference, the same Squigulator-derived R10.4
9-mer pore model on both sides, the same SLOW5 files, three seeds, 500 reads per cell, at
Squigulator's default dwell dispersion.

Our figures are true-positive rates at the lowest threshold giving zero false positives on a
composition-matched shuffled control. RawHash2's are correctly-mapped fractions at its own
default operating point, which is \textbf{not} zero-false-positive: 8.4--10.6\% of control reads
are mapped. The comparison is of magnitude, not of level, and we state it as such.

Table~\ref{tab:rules} gives six rules in triplicate.

\textbf{The $\beta = 0$ control is the informative row.} With gap tolerance removed, chaining is
\emph{worse} than the vote table---9.1\% against 14.1\%---as expected when it tracks 24
candidates where the table tracks 256. The improvement is therefore attributable to the
tolerance, not to the change of data structure.

\textbf{The best decision rule is $+35\%$ relative over voting}, 19.0\% against 14.1\%. No rule
we tried exceeded that.

\textbf{Single rules vary by up to 3.8 points across seeds}---the control spans 7.0 to
10.8---comparable to the gaps \emph{between} rules, and the ranges of adjacent rules overlap. Any
comparison between configurations differing by less than roughly four points requires
replication. We learned this the expensive way: an earlier single-run table reported that
increasing look-back from 48 to 128 did not help. It does, by 1.4 points of mean and positively
in every seed; the single run that supported the old claim was a different seed from the other
five rows of the same table.

Even at its best, the decision rule moves accuracy by tens of percent where the gap to be closed
is a factor of five. The deficiency is not here.

\section{A seed-survival law}
\label{sec:law}

\subsection{The model, and the refutation of our own bound}

Let $a$ be the probability that reference and query assign the same quantiser bucket to
corresponding events. A key packs $E$ consecutive events, so a key matches only if all $E$
agree, and expected anchor yield falls as $a^{E}$.

We originally argued this was a \textbf{lower} bound. Two mechanisms induce positive correlation
between per-event agreements: consecutive events derive from overlapping $k$-mers (adjacent
9-mers share eight bases), and every event of a read is normalised by a single shift-and-scale
estimate, so an error in that estimate displaces all of a read's $z$-values together. Under
positive correlation, agreements cluster, raising the probability that a run of $E$ is entirely
in agreement relative to the independent case.

\textbf{That argument is conditional, and the condition fails for most configurations of
interest.} It holds only given an exact correspondence between the two event sequences. A key
window containing a single inserted or deleted event cannot match however well its neighbours
agree. Writing $g$ for the probability that an alignment column is an indel rather than a
matched pair, the governing quantity is
\[ P(\mathrm{key}) \approx (1-g)^{E} \cdot a^{E} \]
and the first factor is absent from the simple form. Where segmentation is fixed-width and dwell
constant, $g$ is small and $a^{E}$ behaves as the lower bound derived above---measured at $1.8\times$
and $5.1\times$ below the direct count in the two such configurations. Where segmentation is
data-dependent or dwell varies, $g$ rises to 0.09--0.21 and $a^{E}$ becomes an
\textbf{over-estimate}, by between $1.9\times$ and $14\times$ across the remaining cells
(Figure~\ref{fig:modelmeas}).

The qualitative content survives---yield falls geometrically in $E$, with a base that is a
measurable property of the quantiser---but the use of $a^{E}$ as a one-sided bound is restricted
to the exact-correspondence case.

\subsection{An estimator-symmetric instrument}

An agreement figure computed two different ways for two systems is not a comparison. We
therefore emit per-event quantised symbols from both systems in one format and score them with
one program, which does not know which system produced its input.

Our symbols come from the production reference-encoding and quantisation paths. RawHash2 ships
\texttt{--out-quantize}, which dumps query-side symbols; its reference path hardcodes the dump
off, so we added a four-line \texttt{--out-quantize-ref} exposing the same facility on the
reference side, and fixed a record-separator defect that makes the stock multi-read output
unparseable.

The scorer aligns the two symbol streams semi-globally---query aligned in full, free end gaps on
the reference, match $+1$, mismatch $-1$, gap $-1$---and reports $a$ under the maximising
alignment, $a$ under the single best constant offset, the indel fraction, and, directly from the
alignment path, the fraction of positions beginning a gap-free all-matching run of $E$ columns.
That last quantity is $P(\mathrm{key})$ \textbf{measured rather than modelled}, which removes
the independence assumption entirely.

\textbf{Validation.} Under the conditions of our earlier per-event diagnostic, the independent
instrument returns a constant-offset agreement of 0.556 against the 0.559 previously published:
different code, same input, agreeing to 0.3 percentage points.

\textbf{A note on estimator choice.} The constant-offset estimator, which our earlier work used,
understates agreement by a factor of four once retention is data-dependent: 0.188 for our frozen
configuration where the correspondence-aware figure is 0.783. Results obtained with it for
detected-event configurations are withdrawn, including the claim that detection roughly halves
agreement. It does not.

\textbf{The gap is large and it is before seeding.} At CV 0.44, measured key-match probability
differs by a factor of \textbf{46} (0.254 against 0.0055) and anchor supply by a factor of
\textbf{31} (467 against 14.9 per read, the two ratios differing because the systems retain
different numbers of events per read; Table~\ref{tab:agree}). A 31-fold
difference in anchor supply accounts for 91.8\% against 17.6\% without any appeal to the
decision rule.

\textbf{The key-match difference decomposes, and key length is the smaller lever.} Within our
pipeline, measured $P(\mathrm{key})$ at $E = 8$ rather than 12 is 0.0274 against 0.0055, a
factor of \textbf{4.9}. The remaining factor of \textbf{9.3}---0.254 against 0.0274 at the same
key length---is attributable to the encoding and segmentation themselves
($4.9 \times 9.3 = 45.8$, recovering the 46-fold total). Shortening keys is both the smaller
lever and, as Section~\ref{sec:causes} shows, the one that pays for itself in lost specificity.

\textbf{RawHash2's agreement is dwell-invariant where ours is not.} 0.913 $\rightarrow$ 0.911
across CV 0 to 0.44, against 0.797 $\rightarrow$ 0.783 for ours, while our key-match probability
falls $2.2\times$ over the same range because $g$ rises from 0.170 to 0.196. Agreement is not what
moves; correspondence is.

\section{Three root causes}
\label{sec:causes}

\subsection{Asymmetric event retention}

RawHash2 applies its event-merging rule---drop any event whose level differs from the last
retained event by less than \texttt{--sig-diff} $=$ 0.35---\textbf{symmetrically to the
reference encoding and to the query}, retaining 73.4\% on each side. Both sides therefore agree
on how many events a given span contains, by construction.

Our pipeline does not. The reference encoder emits one event per $k$-mer unconditionally; the
query detector emits approximately 0.78. The consequence is measurable and damning: our indel
rate is \textbf{0.170 at zero dwell dispersion}, where there is no timing noise to blame. An
indel rate that high with no noise present is a structural mismatch between two encoders, not a
property of the signal. Because correspondence failure enters $P(\mathrm{key})$ with the same
exponent as disagreement, it costs as much. This is the first thing to fix, and it is a change
to the indexing path rather than a research question.

\subsection{A ${\approx}2.5$-bit quantisation sweet spot}

RawHash2's nominal four bits admit sixteen buckets. Its realised symbol distribution over chr20
occupies six of them---7.7, 21.1, 9.7, 27.6, 24.0 and 8.8 per cent, plus a 0.9 per cent outlier
bucket---for a realised entropy of approximately \textbf{2.46 bits per event}. Its quantiser is
deliberately non-uniform: fine resolution inside a central band, coarse outside.

A third system points the same way, which matters because two points could be coincidence.
Sigmoni~\cite{sigmoni}, which classifies rather than maps and shares none of our decision
machinery, quantises into an alphabet of \textbf{six} symbols by default---2.58 bits---on the
stated grounds that it balances robustness to noise against specificity in exact matching. Two
independent systems landing within a tenth of a bit of each other, one naming noise robustness
as the reason, suggests the operating point is not accidental.

Our uniform quantiser over a clipped $z$-range spends its alphabet evenly, realises more of it,
and agrees less. \textbf{The design axis is per-event entropy against per-event agreement, and
the two systems sit at opposite ends of it.} A key of 8 events at 2.46 bits carries about 19.7
bits of nominal specificity; one of 12 events at nearly 4 realised bits carries about 48. The
system with the \emph{less} specific key is five times more accurate, because specificity it
does not need costs it nothing and agreement it does need costs us everything.

\textbf{Differencing is not the answer, and the reason is instructive.} Encoding successive
level \emph{differences} cancels the shared per-read normalisation shift. Measured in triplicate
it is much worse: 8.3 [3.6--11.8] against 17.6 for the absolute encoding, and worse in every
seed. It retained one symbol per event and changed only what the symbol encoded, so $E$
agreements were still required while each symbol became a function of two noisy levels rather
than one. It attacked the right quantity by the wrong mechanism. What merging does instead is
reduce $E$ \emph{and} raise $a$, which the $(1-g)^{E} a^{E}$ form rewards twice.

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Realised key entropy and occurrence-cap survival, 20 Mb reference.}
\label{tab:entropy}
\centering
\scriptsize
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}
\toprule
geometry & nominal & distinct keys & realised & short & cap \\
\midrule
$3 \times 8$  & 24 & 92,482     & 16.5 & 7.5  & 2.8\%  \\
$4 \times 8$  & 32 & 1,519,844  & 20.5 & 11.5 & 31.2\% \\
$3 \times 13$ & 39 & 5,096,781  & 22.3 & 16.7 & 63.7\% \\
$3 \times 14$ & 42 & 7,985,629  & 22.9 & 19.1 & 78.8\% \\
$4 \times 12$ & 48 & 14,908,778 & 23.8 & 24.2 & 93.5\% \\

\textbf{Specificity is also scale-dependent.} A 39-bit key realises 22.3 bits, a shortfall of
16.7; the frozen 48-bit key realises 23.8, a shortfall of 24.2 (Table~\ref{tab:entropy}). \textbf{The shortfall grows faster than the nominal width}: doubling
nominal key space from 24 to 48 bits buys 7.3 bits of realised entropy.

Short keys saturate the occurrence cap, and worse on larger references. A $3 \times 8$ geometry
keeps only 2.8\% of minimizer occurrences on the 20 Mb reference---97.2\% truncated---and 0.7\%
on the 64 Mb one, 99.3\% truncated. Short keys degrade faster than the reference grows, so a
geometry chosen on a small reference does not transfer to a large one. This is why raising
anchor yield by shortening keys fails: realised entropy collapses before the yield becomes
useful.

\subsection{Recoverable loss inside the chainer}

The correspondence-aware measurement revises our frozen configuration's anchor supply from a
modelled 1.85 per read---derived from the simple $a^{E}$ form for a \emph{fixed-width}
configuration we do not ship---to a measured \textbf{14.9} for the configuration we do. The
observed median best-chain score is \textbf{4}.

So roughly 11 of 15 anchor-eligible positions per read are not reaching the best chain. This loss
was invisible while the estimate sat \emph{below} the observation: a decision stage cannot
recover more anchors than exist, and 1.85 against 4 left no room for loss. The candidates are the
occurrence cap discarding anchors before chaining, the 24-slot greedy chainer thrashing, and a
chaining band of 12 against a measured indel rate of 0.196. We have not isolated which.

This qualifies, but does not overturn, the location of the deficiency. Closing a 31-fold supply
gap dominates recovering a factor of under four. But the decision stage is no longer blameless,
and because the anchors are known to exist, this is a diagnostic rather than a search.

\section{Discussion}
\textbf{Measure $a$ and $g$ before proposing a decision rule.} Both are a single pass over
paired reference and query events, with no training and no search, and together they
establish whether \emph{any} decision rule can succeed before one is designed. A reported
decision rule unaccompanied by reported agreement and correspondence figures cannot be
assessed by a reader. \textbf{Optimise key-match probability, not agreement alone}:
correspondence failure enters with the same exponent as disagreement, and our indel rate is
0.170 with no timing noise present. The currency available to buy both is alphabet, which
RawHash2 and Sigmoni spend and we hoard.

\textbf{Report distributions against derived budgets}, because under a deadline a mean inside
the budget is consistent with any miss rate; we report nine runs with full ranges and name
the one that crosses. And \textbf{run the external baseline first, not last}. Every
intervention we made on the decision stage was measured against our own earlier numbers,
which rose and fell credibly and gave no indication that the ceiling lay elsewhere. One run
of a published tool on identical input would have established within a day that the gap was a
factor of five and not a tuning problem. In a pipeline whose stages are ordered, an internal
improvement series measures progress against the wrong denominator until an external
reference fixes the scale.

\section{Limitations and threats to validity}
\label{sec:limits}

\textbf{Every latency figure was taken under a hypervisor.} WSL2 can deschedule a vCPU
mid-decision, indistinguishable in the data from a slow decision. We treat p50 and p90 as
properties of the implementation and p99 and above as upper bounds contaminated by the
platform; the 2.0--59.4 ms spread of observed maxima, uncorrelated with p99, is the direct
evidence. A deadline-miss rate against the 1.56 ms bound requires bare metal with isolated
cores, tickless operation, interrupt affinity moved off the measured cores and a fixed
governor. We did not have it, and no claim here depends on the tail.

\textbf{All signal is simulated}, from two generators whose detector calibrations do not
transfer to each other by a factor of thirty, and every figure derives from a single
reference, human chr20. Agreement is measured at two dwell levels, one seed, 200 reads per
cell, where accuracy is swept at six levels in triplicate, so the claim that RawHash2's
agreement is dwell-invariant rests on two points. The alignment-based agreement figures are
upper bounds, computed under the correspondence that maximises matches; indel fractions of
0.055--0.208 mean the alignments are near-diagonal, so the estimator is not manufacturing
matches through heavy gapping, but the bound is one-sided and the asymmetry favours RawHash2.
The symmetric-retention explanation is visible in RawHash2's source and consistent with every
measurement, but the decisive ablation---applying our detector to our own reference encoding
and re-measuring---was not made. RawHash2, Squigulator, readfish and Icarust were built and
run here; claims about UNCALLED, Sigmap, RawAlign and Sigmoni rest on their publications and
repositories rather than on execution.

\section{Conclusion}

We set out to determine whether the adaptive-sampling decision can be made in microseconds. It
can: a median of 124.8 µs at genome scale against a 1.56 ms physical budget, with bounded
per-channel state, no allocation on the decision path, and no drops at the offered rate---while
the orchestration layer alone of a standard basecalling client costs 124.3 µs per read-chunk
before any decision is made. The decision budget is not the obstacle to signal-space adaptive
sampling.

The question we answer better than the one we asked is why that is insufficient. Quantised-event
matching is bounded not by the rate at which decisions can be made but by the fidelity with which
signal survives segmentation and quantisation, captured by two measurable quantities whose
$E$-fold product governs everything downstream. At the agreement and correspondence our pipeline
achieves, no decision rule placed after quantisation can recover what segmentation and
quantisation discard---which is why six attempts to place one moved accuracy by at most 35\%
relative against a gap of a factor of five.

That is a negative result about this system and a positive one about where to look. We state it
without apology: a system that fails for a reason that is measured, modelled, and shown to
account for the failure of six attempts to fix it is of more use to the next designer than one
that works for reasons its author cannot name.

\section*{Reproducibility}

All code, data and scripts are in the accompanying repository at commit \texttt{eb0ea28}.
\texttt{scripts/verify\_thesis\_numbers.py} recomputes every number from files under
\texttt{results/}, or, for figures describing code that no longer exists, checks them against the
commit message that recorded them; it exits non-zero on any disagreement, and reports 143 claims
agreeing and none disagreeing. \texttt{scripts/verify\_paper\_numbers.py} performs the same check
against this manuscript. \texttt{scripts/generate\_thesis\_figures.py} regenerates every data
figure from \texttt{results/} and nothing else, byte-stably. Five claims are not settled by any
committed file and are documented as scope boundaries: a bare-metal deadline-miss rate, real
instrument data, agreement across the full dwell sweep and across seeds, the Icarust accept rates
behind the simulator comparison, and the index resident set at minimizer window 10.
